rules.name: Voice reaches the normalizer
rules.where: Phonemizer.phonemize and TextNormalizer.normalize(_:skippingMarkedSpans:), normalize(_:), applyRules
rules.trigger: Infrastructure. TextNormalizer has no voice today, and several rules below read differently for US and GB. Add a british parameter to both normalize entry points, pass Phonemizer.british, and build two rule lists once (rulesUS and rulesGB from one makeRules(british:) function) instead of a shared mutable flag, because phonemizers run on different queues.
rules.reads_as: Nothing by itself.
rules.risks: None in prose. Every GB reading below depends on it, and SpeechTest already phonemizes each case per voice, so tests pin both.

rules.name: Numeric dates with a year
rules.where: TextNormalizer rules: a new rule placed before the phone-number rule (fix3/reading), the file-path rule, the ISO rule, the range rule, the clock and ratio rules and the fraction rules
rules.trigger: A sep B sep YEAR: A and B are 1-2 digits, and sep is the same one of / . - both times. Not preceded by a letter, a digit, _ / . - – − : # @ or a currency sign. Not followed by a letter or digit, by / . - plus a digit, by : plus a digit, or by . plus a letter (a file name: 3-4-2024.pdf). YEAR is four digits 1000-2099 with / or -. With dots the year must be 1900-2099, and the date must not come right after a version word (version, ver, v, build, release, firmware, update, patch, rev, revision, kernel, driver; any case). A two-digit YEAR (01-99) is allowed only with /, and only when A or B has a leading zero (03/04/24) or the word right before is a date word (on, by, until, till, from, since, before, after, due, dated, date, born, died, expires, expiry, exp, expired, signed, issued, effective, valid, through, thru, starting, ending, paid, posted, updated, shipped, delivered). It is never a date when a count or unit word follows (days, weeks, months, years, hours, minutes, seconds, mins, hrs, sizes, mm, cm, inches, times, points). Year 00 leaves the whole thing alone. Order: A 13-31 with B 1-12 is day-month. B 13-31 with A 1-12 is month-day. When both are 1-12 the voice decides (US month-day, GB day-month). Anything else is left alone. Check the day against the month (30-day months, February up to 29).
rules.reads_as: US 'Month Nth, YEAR': 3/4/2024 becomes March 4th, 2024. GB 'the Nth of Month, YEAR': the 3rd of April, 2024, without our 'the' if the word before is already 'the'. Day and month lose leading zeros. A four-digit year stays as digits for the lexicon's year reader. A two-digit year 0N becomes 'oh N'; any other stays the bare number (24 reads twenty-four). Put a comma before the year.
rules.risks: It must run before the phone rule, which today reads 03-04-2024 as 'zero three, zero four, two zero two four'. The two-digit-year limits keep out sizes and option lists (8/10/12, 2/4/12 months, 10/20/30, 5/10/15 minutes, all frozen). The dotted limits keep out versions and builds (1.2.24, 3.4.12, Firmware 2.1.1024). Hyphens need a four-digit year, so 4-4-2 stays. The lookarounds keep out IP addresses, URL paths and file names. Two risks remain: part numbers shaped like dates (10-12-2024), and a dotted build number ending in 19xx or 20xx with no version word before it. Because the voice decides, the British voice reads a US-written 9/11/2001 as 'the ninth of November'.

rules.name: Year-first dates with slashes
rules.where: TextNormalizer: extend the existing ISO-date rule; place it before the numeric-date rule's slash form
rules.trigger: YYYY/M/D or YYYY/MM/DD with a year 1000-2099, a month 1-12 and a valid day. The same lookarounds as the ISO rule, and no / directly before or after. Two groups (the 2023/24 season) are never a date. Dotted year-first forms (2024.3.1) are not accepted: that is calendar versioning (IntelliJ 2024.3.1).
rules.reads_as: Always year-month-day: US 'March 4th, 2024', GB 'the 4th of March, 2024'.
rules.risks: Blog URLs (example.com/2024/03/04/post) are kept out by the slash lookarounds. Frozen cases pin both that and the two-group season.

rules.name: British wording for ISO and month-first dates
rules.where: TextNormalizer: the existing ISO rule and the existing 'Jan 5' rule
rules.trigger: The existing triggers. GB only: the ISO rule emits 'the Nth of Month, YEAR'. The 'Jan 5' rule emits 'Month the Nth'. For GB it also accepts a day already written with st/nd/rd/th (March 5th) so that it can insert 'the'. Insert 'the' only when one of these follows: a comma and a year; one of , ; : ! ? ) or a full stop; the end of the text; or a lower-case function word (the day-first rule's list). Also insert it when a weekday comes right before the month (Sat, Mar 5 works). Never insert it when 'the', 'a', 'an', 'this', 'that', 'its' or a possessive comes right before the month (Meet the March 15 deadline).
rules.reads_as: GB: 2024-03-15 reads the fifteenth of March, twenty twenty-four. Jan 5, 2024 reads January the fifth, twenty twenty-four. March 5th reads March the fifth. The March 15 deadline stays the March fifteenth deadline. US is unchanged.
rules.risks: Only the GB wording changes. The follower test leaves an ordinal before a noun alone (In March 2nd place went to Leeds, frozen), and the attributive test leaves 'the March 15 deadline' alone (speech case). Needs product sign-off (open question).

rules.name: Counts and scores after a month are not days (tighten the existing 'Jan 5' rule)
rules.where: TextNormalizer: the existing 'Jan 5' rule
rules.trigger: Leave the number as it is, with no ordinal, in three cases. First, the month comes right after 'in' or 'In' and no comma and year follows the number. Second, the number is followed by 'of us', 'of them' or 'of you'. Third, the number starts a score: the range rule has already turned 'N-M' into 'N to M', with M smaller than N.
rules.reads_as: In March 2 people left reads In March two people left (today 'March second people'). in May 3-1 reads in May three to one (today 'May third to one'). May 2 of us join? reads May two of us join? (today 'May second of us').
rules.risks: This changes existing readings, but only where they are wrong. Writers rarely put a date after 'in' (the idiom is 'on March 5'), and 'in Jan 5, 2024' still reads as a date because of its year. 'Jan' as a given name before a number (I owe Jan 5 dollars) stays a known false positive of the existing rule.

rules.name: Day-first written dates
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the range rule and before the existing 'Jan 5' and 'Feb.' rules
rules.trigger: A day 1-31, optionally with st/nd/rd/th and optionally a day range (D–D or D-D), then a space and a capitalised month name or abbreviation (Jan through Dec or Sept, optional period). Not preceded by a letter, a digit, . , : / or a currency sign. Not right after a numeral noun (Track, Chapter, Part, Section, Page, Room, Item, Step, Episode, Platform, Gate: the numeralNouns set, any case). It must be followed by one of: an optional comma and a four-digit year; one of , ; : ! ? ) or a full stop; the end of the text or line; a lower-case function word (the, at, in, on, to, until, till, from, and, or, through, when, with, for, by, but, as, is, was, will, we, it, this, that, he, she, they); or 'I'.
rules.reads_as: Both voices: 'the Nth of Month', plus ', YEAR' when there is one. A range reads 'the Nth to the Mth of Month'. Drop our 'the' if the word before is already 'the'. After a weekday: 'Tuesday the 5th of March'. Sometimes the month's abbreviation period is also the full stop: at the end of the text, or when the next word is capitalised and isn't a weekday, month or time word. Then keep a period after the month name: 1 Dec. reads the 1st of December. The existing 'Feb.' rule needs the same fix: today a sentence-final 'Dec.' loses its full stop and with it the sentence's final fall.
rules.risks: The follower list keeps out counts before month-named nouns: We ran 3 March events; 3 April deadlines and 2 May ones; the 4 March sisters; Top 5 May Releases (all frozen). The numeral-noun check keeps out Track 4 March to the Scaffold, where 'to' follows the month. The rule must run before the range rule, or 5–7 March becomes '5 to 7 March'. Misses (On 5 March Parliament voted) are accepted.

rules.name: Month-first day ranges
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the range rule
rules.trigger: A capitalised month name or abbreviation, a space, then D–D or D-D with both 1-31 and the second larger, followed by a non-digit. A smaller second number is a score and is left to the range rule and the tightened 'Jan 5' rule (May 3-1).
rules.reads_as: US 'March 5th to 7th'. GB 'March the 5th to the 7th'.
rules.risks: Today the range rule runs first, and the 'Jan 5' rule then adds 'th' to the first number only, so it reads 'March fifth to seven'. Low risk, because a month word is required.

rules.name: Abbreviated month before a year
rules.where: TextNormalizer: next to the existing 'Feb.' rule
rules.trigger: A capitalised Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Sept, Oct, Nov or Dec (optional period), then a space and a four-digit year 1000-2099 not followed by a digit.
rules.reads_as: The full month name: Jan 2024 reads January twenty twenty-four (today 'jan').
rules.risks: Jan as a given name right before a four-digit number. Rare.

rules.name: Month ranges
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule
rules.trigger: Two capitalised month names or abbreviations (optional periods), each a whole word, joined by - – or — with optional spaces. Not when the pair is followed by romance, relationship, marriage, couple or affair (the May-December idiom).
rules.reads_as: Jan–Mar reads January to March; May-June reads May to June.
rules.risks: The second part must also be a month, so names and places with a month-like first part are left alone: Mar-a-Lago, Jun-ho, Jan-Erik and May-Britt (all frozen). A May-December romance is frozen.

rules.name: Weekday ranges
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the clock and meridiem rules
rules.trigger: Two weekday abbreviations (Mon, Tue, Tues, Wed, Weds, Thu, Thur, Thurs, Fri, Sat, Sun, optional period) joined by - – or — with optional spaces. With these dashes, each side may be in any case: both sides must be weekdays, and unshout may already have lower-cased a shouted MON. When joined by ' to ', ' through ' or ' thru ', both sides must be Title case or ALL CAPS: lower-case 'sat to sun' is a verb and a verb. Also two full weekday names joined by - or –.
rules.reads_as: Mon–Fri reads Monday to Friday in both voices; 'through' and 'thru' read through. Monday-Friday reads Monday to Friday.
rules.risks: Mon-Khmer and Sun-Times are left alone because the second part isn't a weekday. 'The cat sat to sun itself' is left alone because both words are lower case (frozen). Today Mon–Fri reads 'moan, free' and MON-FRI spells F-R-I.

rules.name: Weekday lists
rules.where: TextNormalizer: next to the weekday-range rule
rules.trigger: Two or more Title-case or ALL CAPS weekday abbreviations separated only by ', ', ' & ', ' and ' or '/'. Never lower case.
rules.reads_as: Each one is expanded: Mon, Wed, Fri reads Monday, Wednesday, Friday; Tue/Thu reads Tuesday Thursday (the slash is already silent).
rules.risks: Every item must be a weekday abbreviation. 'He sat, sun on his face' is lower case and frozen.

rules.name: Weekday before a date or time
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the fraction rules, the clock rule and the meridiem rule
rules.trigger: A Title-case or ALL CAPS weekday abbreviation (optional period, optional comma), then a space and one of: a day number and a month (5 March, 12 Jan); a month and a day (Mar 5); a clock time (9:30, 9am, 9 a.m.); or a yearless D/D. The D/D needs both parts 1-31 and no third group, and must be followed by the end, punctuation, at, @, from, to, until, and, or, or a clock time. Sun is never taken right after 'the' or any capitalised word (The Sun, the Toronto Sun). Mon, Wed, Thu and Sat are not taken right after 'the' or a capitalised word in mid-sentence (Nguyen Thu). ALL CAPS SAT and SUN only count inside a range or list (SAT is also the exam).
rules.reads_as: The full weekday name. After a weekday, a yearless D/D becomes a date with the order logic of the numeric-date rule: US Tue 3/5 reads Tuesday, March 5th; GB reads Tuesday, the 3rd of May.
rules.risks: Sat 3 exams in May is left alone, since no month follows the number. Early closing Wed 1/2 day is left alone, since a noun follows the fraction (frozen). Everywhere else a yearless D/D stays a fraction or a number, as decided.

rules.name: Weekday before an ordinal day
rules.where: TextNormalizer: next to the weekday-before-a-date rule
rules.trigger: A weekday name or abbreviation (as the rule above accepts it), a space, then an ordinal 1st-31st. It must be followed by the end, punctuation, a month name, 'at', or a lower-case function word from the day-first list.
rules.reads_as: Insert 'the': Fri 13th reads Friday the 13th; Monday 5th at noon reads Monday the 5th at noon.
rules.risks: An ordinal before a noun is left alone (The Friday 2nd shift starts late, frozen).

rules.name: Weekday abbreviations that are never words
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule
rules.trigger: Tues, Thurs or Fri in Title case, or tues or thurs in lower case (chat), with an optional period, as a whole word, not followed by a letter, a digit or a hyphen and a letter. Not ALL CAPS on its own: FRI is also an acronym, and shouted signs are covered by the range and list rules. Thur is left out of this rule (the river Thur); it reads only through the range, list and after-a-time-word rules.
rules.reads_as: Tuesday, Thursday, Friday. If the abbreviation's period is also the full stop (the end of the text, or a capitalised next word that isn't a weekday, month or time word), keep a period after the word, as the 'St.' handling does.
rules.risks: Very low. Today Tues reads 'tooz' and Fri reads 'free'. Frozen: The FRI score was high; We hiked along the Thur.

rules.name: Ambiguous weekday abbreviations after a time word
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule
rules.trigger: Mon, Tue, Wed, Weds, Thu, Thur, Sat or Sun (Title case, optional period), right after one of: on, by, until, till, til, from, every, next, last, this, before, after, since, each. One space between them and no punctuation. Sun takes only on, every, next, last, this, until, till, each. What follows must be the end of the text, punctuation, or one of: at, morning, afternoon, evening, night, and, or, to, through, a number or a clock time. Never when a hyphen or a capitalised word follows.
rules.reads_as: on Wed reads on Wednesday; every Sun reads every Sunday; next Thu reads next Thursday.
rules.risks: Elsewhere these are words or names: Sat and Wed (verbs), Sun (the star, a newspaper, a company), Thu (a Vietnamese name), Mon (a people, Mon Dieu). The follower test keeps out a name before a verb (After Thu spoke, Lan read the minutes) and a compound (this Sun-like star), both frozen. Misses (on Wed we decided) are accepted.

rules.name: Relative timestamps with 'ago'
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the units rule (see risks about the lexicon)
rules.trigger: A whole number not preceded by a letter, a digit, . , or a currency sign, an optional space, then s, m, h, d, w, wk, wks, mo, mos or y (lower case only), then a space and 'ago'.
rules.reads_as: N second(s), minute(s), hour(s), day(s), week(s), month(s) or year(s) ago, singular for 1. 5m ago reads five minutes ago; 1w ago reads one week ago.
rules.risks: Without 'ago', nothing is touched: 5m means metres or millions, 3d is 3D, 2d an array, 2H a pencil grade, 21h hex and 10s a decade (all frozen or guarded). The money rule already takes '$5m ago'. If the units work makes 'm' a custom-lexicon unit entry (as mm is), the lexicon will mark 5m before this rule runs. Then either make this rule a pre-lexicon pass in Phonemizer, or skip unit entries followed by ' ago'. Feed stamps without 'ago' (· 5m) stay as they are.

rules.name: Time units missing from the units table
rules.where: TextNormalizer.units
rules.trigger: Add wk/wks (week/weeks), mo/mos (month/months) and mth/mths (month/months) to the after-a-number units table. (yr and yrs already landed with fix3/reading.)
rules.reads_as: 6 mos reads six months (today 'moes'); 3 wks reads three weeks (today spelled out).
rules.risks: The money per-unit rule already takes '/mo' after an amount, earlier in the list. Adjectival use (a 6 mo lease) gets the plural, the same known limitation as other units.

rules.name: Compound durations
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the units rule and the 'range with a unit on both numbers' rule
rules.trigger: Two or three number-and-unit parts with units from d, h (or hr/hrs), m (or min/mins) and s (or sec/secs), lower case only. They must be in strictly falling order (d, h, m, s), glued or one space apart, with at least one single-letter unit. Every part after the first is under 60 (hours under 24 after days). When the first part is m and s follows directly, the m part must also be under 60. Not preceded by a letter, a digit, . , or :, and not followed by a letter or digit.
rules.reads_as: 1h 30m reads 1 hour 30 minutes; 2h30m reads 2 hours 30 minutes; 1h 30m 15s reads 1 hour 30 minutes 15 seconds; 2d 4h reads 2 days 4 hours. No 'and', as specified.
rules.risks: A lone 2h or 30m is never read here. Lower case keeps out pencil grades (4H and 2B, frozen). The under-60 rule for m keeps out a sprint written 100m 10s. The order and value limits keep out codes and coordinates.

rules.name: Hours:minutes:seconds
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the clock-time and ratio rules
rules.trigger: H:MM:SS with hours 0-23 (one or two digits) and minutes and seconds exactly two digits, 00-59. Not preceded by a digit, :, . or ,. Not followed by a digit, by :, by . or , plus a digit (subtitle files), or by a letter (40:26:46N).
rules.reads_as: It is a clock time when the word before is 'at' or '@', a date comes right before it, am/pm or a time-zone word follows, the hour is 13 or more, or it opens a line or sits in square brackets (a log stamp, [09:15:02]). A clock time reads HH:MM as the clock rule does, plus 'and N seconds' unless the seconds are 00: at 06:30:00 reads six thirty; at 14:32:07 reads fourteen thirty-two and seven seconds. Otherwise it is a duration: 'N hours N minutes N seconds', with zero parts dropped (1:00:00 reads one hour; 00:01:30 reads one minute thirty seconds) and plurals by value.
rules.risks: Ratios (1:2:4), four-group timecodes (01:02:03:04) and coordinates (51:30:26 N, hours over 23) are left alone (all frozen). A morning log stamp that is neither in brackets nor at the start of a line still reads as a duration.

rules.name: Century abbreviations
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule
rules.trigger: An ordinal 1st to 21st (digits plus st/nd/rd/th), an optional space or hyphen, then 'c.' or 'cent.' as a whole word. A capital 'C.' counts only with its period and only when 'the' comes right before the ordinal (the 17th C.).
rules.reads_as: 18th c. reads 18th century; 18th-c. reads 18th-century. If the period is also the full stop (the end of the text, or a capitalised next word), keep one: 'century.'.
rules.risks: '5th C' is a school class section in Indian English (frozen: My son is in 5th C this year). 'c. 1850' (circa) is not touched (frozen); that belongs to the academic pack.

rules.name: Quarter or half followed by an apostrophe year
rules.where: Phonemizer.phonemize: a pre-lexicon pass next to linkLabels and foldMicroSign, because the custom lexicon marks Q1-Q4, H1, H2 and FY before TextNormalizer runs
rules.trigger: Q1-Q4, H1, H2 or FY, not preceded by a letter or digit, followed directly by an apostrophe (straight or curly) and two digits, with no letter, digit or apostrophe after them.
rules.reads_as: Insert a space: Q3'24 becomes Q3 '24, which already reads Q three twenty-four (as Q4 '23 does today). A '05 then gets the short-year rule (oh five).
rules.risks: None. Today the marked Q3 and '24 run together as one word. A possessive (Q3's) is left alone (frozen).

rules.name: Time ranges with am/pm
rules.where: TextNormalizer: a new rule placed before the clock-time and '5pm' rules (this may belong to whoever owns clock times)
rules.trigger: H or H:MM with optional am/pm, then - or – (optional spaces), then H or H:MM with am/pm. Hours 1-12.
rules.reads_as: 9am–5pm reads 9 AM to 5 PM; 10-4pm reads 10 to 4 PM. Today the dash is a pause and there is no 'to'.
rules.risks: Low. Its one speech case (Open Mon–Sat, 10am–6pm.) spells AM and PM as 'ay em' and 'pee em', as the seed file does. It only passes once the harness joins spelled letter names (see review notes).

rules.name: British 'and' in years 2001-2009
rules.where: Lexicon.getNumber: the four-digit year branch (NumberWords.year), British voice only
rules.trigger: A four-digit year 2001-2009 read by the GB voice.
rules.reads_as: two thousand and five (US stays two thousand five).
rules.risks: This overlaps the numbers area: GB cardinals have no 'and' at all today (205 reads two hundred five). Agree it with that area before landing (open question).

open_questions: British voice: should a date written month first (March 5, Jan 5, 2024) read 'March the fifth', and an ISO date read 'the fifteenth of March'? Recommend yes. Oxford Learner's Dictionaries labels 'March the fifth' and 'the fifth of March' as British and 'March fifth' as North American. The British expected readings assume yes. They also assume that a date used before a noun keeps no 'the' (the March fifteenth deadline).

Which signal decides the order of an ambiguous numeric date such as 3/4/2024? Recommend the voice: US reads month first, GB reads day first. It is simple, predictable and easy to test, and a per-user date-order setting could override it later. Know the cost first. The British voice will read a US-written 9/11/2001 as 'the ninth of November'. Dotted dates (3.4.2024) are a day-first convention everywhere they are used, yet the US voice will read them month first, as the brief specifies.

Two-digit years: read them as written (3/4/24 reads March fourth, twenty-four; 05 reads oh five)? Recommend yes, because picking a century is a guess. The review also narrowed when a two-digit year counts as a date: only with a leading zero (03/04/24) or a date word just before it (on, dated, expires…). Otherwise sizes 8/10/12, '2/4/12 months' and '10/20/30' would read as dates. Confirm that narrowing.

Hours:minutes:seconds such as 'Her time was 2:03:59': unit words ('two hours three minutes fifty-nine seconds') or clock style ('two oh three fifty-nine')? Recommend unit words with zero parts dropped. Use clock style after 'at', when the hour is 13 or more, and for bracketed log stamps. For a clock time with seconds ('at 14:32:07'), recommend 'fourteen thirty-two and seven seconds', the BT speaking-clock form.
'1h ago': 'one hour ago' or 'an hour ago'? Recommend 'one hour ago'. It follows the text and matches how every other number reads.
Feed and spec stamps without 'ago' ('Jane · 5m', 'Battery: 18h'): should they read as minutes and hours? Recommend leaving them alone, because 5m also means metres and millions, and 21h can be hex.
American voice: should 'Mon–Fri' read 'Monday to Friday' or 'Monday through Friday'? Recommend 'to' for both voices, as in the brief.

British years 2001-2009 with 'and' ('two thousand and five'), and British numbers with 'and' in general ('two hundred and five')? Recommend yes for years in this area, and ask the numbers owner to decide British cardinals as a whole.

The existing 'Jan 5' rule has false positives that this set now tests: 'In March 2 people left' (today 'March second people'), 'They lost in May 3-1' ('May third to one') and 'May 2 of us join?' ('May second of us'). Approve tightening an existing rule? Recommend yes; the tightening is narrow (after 'in', before 'of us', before a score).

Month-year forms with no day ('Expires 12/2025', a card's 'Exp 08/27'): 'December twenty twenty-five', or leave them as numbers? Recommend leaving them to a later pass. 'Twelve twenty twenty-five' is just as natural, and the two-part slash collides with fractions and scores.
review_notes: Wrong expectation fixed: 'The attacks of 9/11/2001…' had says_gb 'the eleventh of September'. The stated rule (both numbers 12 or under, so the voice decides) gives the British voice 'the ninth of November'. The case is now US-only, and the cost is recorded in the order open question.

Wrong expectation fixed: 'Sat, Mar 5 works for me' expected British 'March the fifth', but the GB 'the' rule as written needed a function word to follow, and 'works' isn't one. The rule now also inserts 'the' after a weekday. It also gained an attributive guard, because as written it would have produced 'the March the fifteenth deadline'. A new speech case pins that guard: 'Meet the March 15 deadline.' reads 'March fifteenth' in both voices.

Tightened rules, each with new frozen near-misses (29 new frozen cases in total). Two-digit-year dates now need a leading zero or a date word, because sizes 8/10/12, ages '2/4/12 months', '10/20/30' and '5/10/15 minutes' would have become dates. Dotted dates now need a year from 1900 and no version word before them (Firmware 2.1.1024). Day-first dates now skip numeral nouns (Track 4 March to the Scaffold). Weekday ranges joined by 'to' and weekday lists no longer accept lower case ('sat to sun itself'; 'sat, sun on his face'). Weekday plus D/D now needs a time-like follower (Early closing Wed 1/2 day). Sun is skipped after a capitalised word (Toronto Sun). The never-a-word list dropped Thur (the river) and ALL CAPS on their own (FRI as an acronym). Weekdays after a time word now need a time-like follower and no hyphen (After Thu spoke…; this Sun-like star). Month ranges skip the May-December idiom. H:MM:SS now needs hours 0-23 and two-digit minutes and seconds (1:2:4; 51:30:26 N; four-group timecodes). Century 'C.' needs 'the' first (5th C as a school section). Compound durations are lower case only (4H and 2B pencils). The Q'YY split needs two digits (Q3's).

New findings in existing behaviour. The existing 'Jan 5' rule rewrites counts and scores: 'In March 2 people left' reads 'March second people', 'They lost in May 3-1' reads 'May third to one', and 'May 2 of us join?' reads 'May second of us'. I added these as speech cases with a narrow tightening rule. 'I owe Jan 5 dollars' (Jan as a name) is noted but not tested. The existing 'Feb.' rule swallows a sentence-final full stop ('…is 24 Dec.' has no final period in the output), so the sentence loses its final fall. The harness can't see this because loose() drops punctuation; it's written into the day-first rule.

New positive cases from realistic text: British and US quoted-email headers ('On Mon, 4 Mar 2024 at 10:15, Jane Doe wrote:'), a receipt line with a 24-hour time, a date-of-birth field, a British formal date with a full weekday, 'Effective 1 Jan 2025', a news byline mixing a day-first date with '3h ago', 'Posted Thu 14 Mar 2024', 'Term starts Mon 2 Sept.', 'Open Tues–Sun', shop hours with am/pm, chat 'See you thurs!', 'Every Thurs at 7', 'See you Fri 13th' (new small rule: weekday before an ordinal takes 'the'), 'Paid on 3/4/24', 'Runtime: 1:45:00', 'Bake for 1h 5m', 'From the Toronto Sun, 9 March 2024', plus regression guards that already pass ('March 1st, 2024', 'the 1st of May', '1800s', Q4 '23).

Removed frozen cases. 'Plan A starts at 9.' pins another area's reading of 'A' (a schwa today) and isn't a date near-miss. 'Monday was busy.', 'In 1999 we left.', 'Meet at 6:00.', 'At 10:05 we left.', 'COVID-19 cases rose.', 'Ages 18–25 apply.', 'They won 3-1 at home.' and 'About 1/3 of us came.' were duplicates or not near-misses for any rule here. A few kept frozen cases pin readings other areas might change later ('Latitude 51:30:26 N', 'Cut at 01:02:03:04', 'Early closing Wed 1/2 day'); their notes say to refreeze if those areas land.

Verification. Every says and says_gb line was phonemized in both voices: none came back unknown and none were misread ('queue' gives the same phonemes as Q; Thursday, Wednesday, eighteenth century, oh five and nineteen eighty-seven are fine). Frozen texts were phonemized as well. On a scratch copy with number hyphens turned into spaces, the harness passes 30 voice-checks for behaviour that exists today: US ISO, Jan 5, March 1st, March 5th, Sept. 12, the March 15 deadline, the 1st of May, 5 mins, 1 hr, 1hr 30min, 90 min, '05, '90s, 1990s, 1800s, Q4 '23, US 2005 and £5m. Every other check fails only because its rule doesn't exist yet. No repo files were edited.

Harness blocker, confirmed again. SpeechTest keeps word spaces, and a hyphenated number word in says is read as one word: 'twenty-four' gives twˈɛntifˌɔɹ while 24 gives twˈɛnti fˈɔɹ, and British 'ninety-nine' gives nˌIntɪnˈIn against nˈInti nˈIn. Any case with a tens-and-units word in says, including the seed's 'It costs four ninety-nine.', can't pass until this is fixed. Letter names have the same problem: 'ay em' and 'pee em' give two words, but AM gives one (ˌAˈɛm). That is why the seed's own 'I ate M&Ms at 5 pm.' fails. Suggested fix in Sources/ReadAloud/SpeechTest.swift, applied to says and says_gb before phonemizing: turn a hyphen between a tens word and a units or ordinal word into a space, and join a run of two or more spelled letter names (ay, bee, see, …, em, pee) into capital letters. The cases keep hyphens and spelled letters, as the format asks.

Size. There are 106 speech cases and 76 frozen cases, above the 40-80 and 30-60 targets. The extra cases are cheap regression guards and the new near-misses. If the parent needs to trim, drop the pure regression guards first (1800s, Q4 '23, '90s, the 1st of May).
